6. How Jolly, a placeholder avatar, became an icon

episodes.title: How a 19-year-old intern built the growth engine behind this $2B AI company | Hector Serrano
episodes.description:
Hector Serrano runs one of the most innovative and successful paid growth programs in Silicon Valley. As Head of Content at Wispr Flow, a leading AI voice-to-text tool, he built a roster of 50 creators who drive 500 to 600 paid user-generated content (UGC) ads every month. The creators are paid a cut of ad spend, and the best of them earn over $13,000 a month. It’s a playbook the best DTC brands have used for years, now adapted for SaaS. Hector joined Wispr Flow at 19, before the product had PMF, and over the past year, Wispr Flow has grown revenue 30x and raised at a $2 billion valuation.
We discuss:
1. Why paid UGC is one of the biggest untapped growth levers right now
2. The step-by-step playbook for building a successful paid-UGC program
3. Why the best marketers are “allergic to AI”
4. What makes a great modern marketing hire
5. Why YouTube is the most underrated growth lever in SaaS

episodes.title: An 86-minute guide to finding PMF | Rob Snyder (Author, The Power of Pull)
episodes.description:
Rob Snyder is the author of The Power of Pull and writes the newsletter The Physics of Startups. He has advised more than 50 startups on growing from zero to $1 million in ARR, drawing on his own experience as a founder who spent two years pushing a product the market didn’t want before accidentally stumbling onto what actually works. In this episode, we walk step by step through his framework for finding product-market fit, from coming up with an idea to closing your first handful of deals.
We discuss:
1. The PULL framework: Project, Unavoidable, List of options, Limitations
2. Where the best startup ideas come from
3. Tactics for cold outreach and running your first sales call
4. Why Rob advises against design partners
5. Goblin mode: what to do when nothing is working
6. How to apply the PULL framework inside larger companies

episodes.title: Inside the black box of AI: How AI models actually think | Emmanuel Ameisen (Anthropic)
episodes.description:
Emmanuel Ameisen is an interpretability researcher at Anthropic, where he looks inside LLMs like Claude to understand how they think. Before joining Anthropic, he spent years in applied ML at Stripe and Insight, and is the author of Building Machine Learning Powered Applications. His research has produced some of the most striking findings in the field: that models form general representations of concepts, plan many tokens ahead without stating those plans explicitly, and may exhibit something structurally similar to the distinction between conscious and unconscious processing in humans.
We discuss:
1. Why the “next-token predictor” framing undersells how models actually plan and think
2. Why anthropomorphizing AI can actually be the right approach
3. Why models are “grown,” not built
4. What the “J space” reveals about model self-awareness
5. The smooth scaling curve behind what look like sudden capability jumps
6. How interpretability connects to AI alignment and safety

episodes.title: Why every company now needs to think and operate like a lab team | Josh Woodward (Google Labs, Gemini, AI Studio)
episodes.description:
Josh Woodward is the head of Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio. He has spent over 17 years at Google and oversees its longest-running and largest labs team, whose products include NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook), Project Genie, and Flow. His job is to find, experiment with, and scale new AI products, and he has built one of the most distinctive product cultures in the industry for generating ideas, running experiments, and, even more importantly, knowing when to quit.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why every company now needs to think and operate like a labs team
2. Where the best ideas really come from
3. The “almost possible” framework
4. How to recognize genuine product-market fit early
5. When to kill an idea
6. What skills are rising in value in the AI era
7. Why roles are not actually blurring into one universal builder role
8. How to set up your internal labs team

episodes.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
episodes.description:
A camera moves around a person. Halfway around, the model has to draw the back of a head it has never seen. How much can it learn about that missing view just by watching video? That’s the question we put to Andreas Blattmann and Dustin Podell of Black Forest Labs.
Their answer runs through FLUX 3. BFL trained one backbone on images, video and audio. The guests explain what each adds, how they decide which parts of denoising deserve the most compute, and why a detail that looks great in a still can flicker from frame to frame. We also get into the case for autoregression and where they think diffusion still has an edge.
There’s personal history here. Stable Diffusion is why Dustin left his software job and why swyx started Latent Space. They revisit the first FLUX training run in a French chalet, the photo experiment behind FLUX Kontext, and some of the things people actually use these models for, from restoring old family photos to generating a clip with synchronized sound.
This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Deepgram is the voice AI infrastructure behind natural conversation—bringing speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice-focused LLMs, and agents to teams building with voice AI.

episodes.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
episodes.description:
A coding agent opens a pull request and picks an email provider for you. How did it choose? Resend co-founder and CEO Zeno Rocha explores answer engine optimization (AEO) through a concrete example: which email provider does Claude Code recommend, and how does that change across model versions? Then comes the agent experience itself. Once the agent picks Resend, can it find the price, set up the account and send its first email?
We also follow an email after the API call succeeds. Zeno explains what happens when Gmail throttles a burst, why a tracking pixel can give you the wrong idea about who opened a message, and how one abusive sender can put other customers’ mail at risk. Then we get into the product decisions: giving an agent 80+ named MCP tools, letting it read pricing in Markdown, and letting it register for a service on its own.

episodes.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team
episodes.description:
Our first deep dive with an AI data company. Handshake AI went from launch to roughly $1 billion in annualized gross revenue in about a year. What are frontier labs actually buying? Garrett Lord and the team open up the reinforcement learning environments behind their expert training data, from biology and investment banking to alignment.
An AI agent found a way to earn credit for net income: open a new Excel tab and fill it with every number from one to a million. The grader found the number it wanted. A banker would have looked for it in the right row, for the right year.
Garrett Lord and the Handshake AI team take Latent Space inside the work of building evaluations for frontier labs. A scientist walks us through a gel and nine brain-tissue slides. A banker follows an agent through its inbox, Python code, and financial model to find the assumption that broke the deal. The safety team shows how to read an agent’s actions when its final answer sounds fine.

episodes.title: Rebuilding GitHub for the Agent Era — Jay Parikh, EVP of CoreAI, Microsoft
episodes.description:
GitHub’s next scaling challenge is the agent workload. The platform has 225 million developers and handled 34.3 billion commits over the past year. Jay Parikh, EVP of CoreAI at Microsoft, joins us straight after his GitHub Universe keynote to talk about rebuilding the software-development stack for that scale.
We get into Copilot Fusion’s approach to model orchestration and the quality–cost frontier; the harness underneath it; agents that carry a session across phone, desktop and VS Code; and the infrastructure work behind GitHub’s move to Azure. Jay also makes the case for measuring AI spending against completed work and business outcomes.
Along the way: why Jay skips pull requests in some of his own repos, Matt Pocock’s repo of Markdown instructions, and the open-source maintenance question behind replacing 2,000 dependencies with 20. Stay for the programmable conference badge at the end.
Before the interview: why agent traffic changes GitHub’s job, Jay’s infrastructure background, and AI Engineer CODE — Nov 10–12 in San Francisco.

• GitHub’s 2026 Octoverse report — The original charts behind the 34.3B commits and agent-first PR figures.
• Matt Pocock’s test-driven development skill — Open the Markdown file in the revision that was current when we recorded.

• Push protection for AI-detected secrets — The actual rejected push and what the developer sees in the terminal.

episodes.title: How Fast Can AI Become an Expert?
AIs might overthrow the government within a year – Paul Christiano
episodes.description:
Paul Christiano is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen).
Paul thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario).
He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails.
He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it.
And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion.

In 1984, the Walt Disney Company was worth more dead than alive. Disney Animation — the heart of Walt's famous flywheel — had stagnated for years, bleeding away talent while corporate raiders circled, salivating over offers to sell off the film library to MGM and offload the parks to hotel operators. But what followed instead was the greatest turnaround in media history under Michael Eisner and Frank Wells. Beauty and the Beast. The Lion King. Broadway. Bringing the Disney Vault home on VHS and DVD. And the greatest media acquisition of all time — ESPN.
And then... it all almost fell apart. Again. Euro Disney turned into a money pit. Boardroom and executive infighting ran rampant. Animation descended into a dumpster fire. (Remember Chicken Little? Us neither.) Comcast — Comcast!! — tried to steal the company via a hostile takeover. Out of the chaos, a new generation of Disney management emerged under Bob Iger to stage yet another epic comeback with Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm, creating the defining media empire of the 21st century…until the tech companies came along. episodes.title: AI Software Factories
episodes.description:
“Clearly there are 100x or 1,000x engineers now. The world hasn’t adjusted.”
— Guillermo Rauch (Vercel)
Guillermo: I’ve been really pilled with this idea of software factories. You used to ship the output directly, and everything inside the company was how good is person A at shipping output B? And now what’s happening is the way that I’m judging you as an engineer is, are you producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z, right?
We used to believe, and it used to be somewhat controversial, that there’s 10X engineers. Now clearly there’s 100X or 1,000X engineers. And the world hasn’t fully adjusted to this.
@naval: I used to get flamed on Twitter for saying there are 10X engineers, because it flies in the face of so much equality philosophy that everyone’s equal. But the reality is, when you’re operating in idea domains—when you’re operating in intellectual domains and virtual digital domains—it’s not even 10X. It’s 100X or 1,000X, and it always has been.
Satoshi, Notch, the guy who invented JavaScript, the Brendan Eichs of the world. John Carmack. These are 1,000X programmers.
Not to even mention if you choose the right thing to work on versus the wrong thing to work on, that’s an infinity difference. And it could just be not necessarily even a better programmer, just one who had a better judgment of what to work on in the first place.
And now obviously it’s less controversial, because of AI leverage.

episodes.description:
I sit down with Ras Mic to see how he runs his work and his life through Grok Bot. He calls himself a Grok Bot maxi, and he uses it as a personal agent and as an orchestrator that hands engineering work to Claude Code. He walks me through five areas: engineering, design, content ideation, business and finance, and shopping. Along the way he shows his bots, his prompts, and the projects they shipped, including Pluto, Bezalel, a Rust trading app, and a Shopify store for his brother's clothing brand. If you ship ideas, this episode gives you a setup you can copy today.
Timestamps
00:00 – Intro
01:55 – Engineering Bot
07:57 – Why use Grok Bot as an Orchestrator
14:01 – Grok Bot + Claude Code
19:43 – Security Checks
21:54 – Designer Bot
31:12 – Content Bot
37:19 – Business & Finance Bot
42:41 – Shopping Bot
44:53 – Closing Thoughts
Key Points
• Give each serious project its own bot, keep one general engineering bot for random ideas, and delete bots once they stop being useful.
• Use Grok Bot to orchestrate and Claude Code with Opus 5.5 to write the code.
• Ras Mic says the $200-a-month Claude Code plan is worth $8,000 to $12,000 in API credits, so he leans on subscriptions.
• Lock the design in Paper before any code gets written, with a design system the agent can reference.
• A YouTube bot scans X at 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. and sends three video topics with tweets, title ideas, and resources.
• Finance bots connected through Plaid give Ras Mic's advisor bot enough context to talk him out of shiny objects.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. Engineering Bot
Grok Bot organizes work into bots, each with its own context, skills, and computer, where the ChatGPT app gives you threads that get mixed up. Ras Mic lets context decide. Pluto, his Bible app, and Bezalel (at $200 MRR) each get a bot, a general engineering bot catches random ideas like Still, a screenshot extension built in two prompts, and permanent bots handle IT and ML. When a bot stops being useful, he right-clicks and deletes it.
2. Grok Bot Orchestrates, Claude Code Builds
Ras Mic sends ideas to his engineering bot at night and wakes up to a repo on GitHub, like the AI governance compliance app it built after a friend told him about government contracting. For Pluto, he had Grok Bot review a plan from a PDF, revise it with his feedback and a friend's, then build it with Claude Code on Opus 5.5 using /goal. The run went for hours and returned five working PRs, which people are now testing.
3. Why Grok Bot + Claude Code
I ask why an engineer would put Grok Bot on top of Claude Code or Codex, and Ras Mic points to the UX. He works through PRs from his phone during dinner at his mom's house and talks to a bot on speaker while he drives. Grok Bot also covers the business side. While building VP Cloud, a Canadian sovereign cloud, one of his bots emailed a GPU provider on its own to ask for a discount and mentioned his YouTube subscriber count.
5. Design Bot
Ras Mic collects inspiration from X and Mobbin, sends a screenshot to his agent, and has it build a design system in Paper through the Paper MCP. He used that flow for his brother's clothing brand, where Grok Bot designed a Christian gothic storefront in Paper and then built it as a Shopify front end.
6. Content Bot
Twice a day, at 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Ras Mic's YouTube bot scans X and sends three topics that fit his channel, each with source tweets, a title idea, and resources. He mostly scripts his own videos because people prefer people, and he uses an editor bot to explore styles and brief his human editor.
7. Advisor Bot
Ras Mic has shiny object syndrome, so he runs ideas past an advisor bot. His finance bots connect to his accounts through Plaid, so the advisor can read his transactions and hold him to his goals. When he sent it a real estate listing, it advised against buying, citing cash pulled from his other goals, a seller who wanted unrepresented buyers only, and a boiler and furnace from 2009.
8. Shopper Bot
Grok Bot scans eBay every day for sealed GPUs. For Ras's PS5 Pro, it emailed the seller, learned it was a store in Ontario two hours away, gave him the number to call, and bought the console once he confirmed. It also found shoes for his sciatica and emailed the list to his wife for approval.

episodes.description:
In this solo episode, I share 12 prompts for Fable 5.2 across four areas: making money, productivity, video and content, and hardware. I run several of them live, including an audit of my design agency, a freelance job Fable 5.2 found on Upwork, a 100-niche research sweep with subagents, and a minimalist phone it designed from one prompt. I cover why Fable 5.2 can work 10 to 12 hours on its own, why it now admits when it lacks an answer, and how to sell results as a fixed-price service. If you want to make money, get more done, or build hardware with Fable 5.2, this episode gives you prompts you can copy today.
Timestamps
00:00 – Intro
01:00 – Prompt 1: Audit Your Entire Business
02:05 – Prompt 2: A Freelance Job End to End
03:46 – Prompt 3: A Hundred Niches at Once
04:33 – Prompt 4: Rebuild the Ancient Software
05:25 – Prompt 5: Deal Checker for a Boring Business
06:54 – Results from Prompts

10:07 – Prompt 8: Red Team My Plan
11:11 – Video and Marketing Engineering
12:39 – Prompt 9: Short-Form Editor
13:05 – Prompt 10: Niche Explainer Videos
13:24 – Prompt 11: One Episode, Every Format
13:56 – Prompt 12: One person Hardware Company
16:42 – A Minimalist Phone Idea
17:41 – Design and Mockups
18:31 – Closing Thoughts
Key Points
• Fable 5.2 works 10 to 12 hours on its own, so I hand it jobs that take a high-end consultant a week.
• Freelance jobs and software rebuilds can now sell per output, where people used to bill by the hour.
• Stronger subagents let me research 100 niches in one prompt and get back one ranked table.
• Fable 5.2 now admits uncertainty, which opens up finance and legal work like checking a seller's P&L.
• Videos at $1 to $5 each let me build faceless channels and own distribution.
• One prompt gets me a parts list, circuit design, firmware, and a printable enclosure for a device.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. Long Jobs and Freelance Work
My audit prompt asks Fable 5.2 to review my website, pricing, onboarding, emails, and top five competitors, keep a running log, and rank the 10 changes most likely to make money, with evidence for each. For LCA, my design agency, it ranked every call with evidence and stayed to the point, as it has on every business we incubate. I asked it to find a freelance job it could do, and it picked an Upwork equity analyst report on TDMX at a $450 fixed price
2. Subagents and Old Software
Fable 5.2 runs many subagents well, so one prompt spins up a subagent for each of 100 niches to find the top three complaints, what people pay today, and how hard each niche is to reach, then returns one ranked table and the five to build for. Another prompt hands it a spreadsheet a client has run their business on for 12 years and asks it to figure out what the sheet does, rebuild it as a simple web app
3. A Model That Admits Uncertainty
Hallucination has held legal and finance teams back from AI, and Fable 5.2 now admits when it lacks an answer, the way a person would. My deal checker prompt hands it a seller's P&L and listing, asks it to flag everything that fails to add up, label each number verified, unverified, or suspicious, and write the 15 questions I should ask before making an offer.
4. Productivity Prompts
The Grill Me prompt interviews me with 20 questions, one at a time, about how I make decisions in my business, then turns my answers into a skill file Fable 5.2 follows from then on. It operates a computer well, so it can open an old invoicing app, export last month's invoices, match them against the bank statement, list outstanding ones, and check with me before sending anything.
5. Video, Content, and Distribution
My three prompts cut a raw four-minute talking-head video to its strongest 45 seconds with three hooks, build a 60-second animated niche explainer with five opening lines, and turn one transcript into a PDF playbook, five tweets in my voice, a newsletter, a two-minute free tool, and flags on any claim that needs a check.
6. Vibe Manufacturing From One Prompt
I recall Anthropic saying in a blog post that Fable 5.2 designed three working devices from a single prompt, so my hardware prompt asks for a one-job device for one niche with a priced parts list, circuit design, firmware, a printable enclosure, and the cost to make 100.

episodes.description:
In this solo episode, I lay out how I think about building an AI-proof business now that anyone can press a few buttons and spin up a company in seconds. Layoffs keep coming, people copy products pixel for pixel, and I still see more opportunity than ever. I walk through eight categories: atoms, permission, attention, timing, belonging, liquidity, unique data, and outcomes. I share examples like Hampton, final.com, and Cars & Bids, say how I'd rank the categories, and show how to mix them. If you're an employee looking at a startup or a founder worried about getting copied, this episode gives you a map for building something with value when AI makes software, content, and answers almost free.

Key Points
• Physical businesses hold up against overnight clones, and I expect their valuations to rise as tech money moves in.
• Licenses, regulation, and preferred-vendor deals are permission that a copycat has a hard time getting on day one.
• Media is underrated, and AI lets you run a content machine around a micro niche.
• A first mover's product may be easy to copy, while the data, brand, and trust it collects stay AI-proof.
• Marketplaces rank among the stickiest businesses of all time, and agents let a team of one to five run one.
Section Summaries
1. Atoms and Permission
Pixels are software businesses and atoms are physical ones, like a coffee shop or the plumber who fixes your clogged toilet. They're harder to run, they hold up against overnight clones, and I think their valuations go up once AI and tech money spots the moat. Permission covers licenses, regulation, and deals, so you could partner with a lawyer and handle marketing, growth, and AI while they run the firm.
3. Attention
Attention is somehow underrated right now, and people follow people. I used to hate making short form video, and now Opus 5.5 is my editor, I create on my own schedule, and I got hundreds of thousands of views in the last week. I'd pick a micro niche and build a media company around it with newsletters, meme pages, or founder-led content, aiming for a trustworthy brand that people come to for that niche.
4. Timing
I see more trends in more micro niches than ever, and sometimes I'm shocked by how few people have built for them. I'd use ideabrowser.com, GrokBot, Claude Duet, or any personal agent platform to monitor your niches, then build first, whether that's software, a physical product, or a media company.
5. Belonging
People are as connected as ever and feel as disconnected as ever, so I see a big opportunity in paid communities built around a shared goal, like a Circle or Skool group or a weekly virtual event that keeps people accountable. As I understand it, my friend Sam Parr's company, Hampton, runs meetups around North America for entrepreneurs doing at least $3 million a year in revenue. We threw an IRL event in Nashville last week for founders deploying agents, and demand ran past what we knew how to meet.
6. Liquidity
People tell me software is done, and marketplaces are the example I give back. A friend of mine launched final.com, I think last week, where you bid every week on curated high-end collectible cars, and he markets it to his big Instagram audience, while Cars & Bids sold for many millions of dollars.
7. Unique Data
You see data brokers making millions of dollars a week, and platforms like, I think, Mercor and micro1 got coding data and sold it to the big models, which stay hungry for new types of data. You can also sell access to a curated directory, and I expect a huge explosion of curated websites and apps as LLMs and social feeds give people infinite content, with polarized, gamed restaurant reviews on Google and Yelp as one example.
8. Outcomes and Mixing the Map
Customers are starting to pay for results through automated AI services, like a creative agency that makes logos and landing pages on the fly or a machine that studies Fiverr and Upwork and bids on the work. Your defense comes from feeding the best possible agents the best data, insights, and inspiration, plus permission like a deal with a particular company.
